a2.RJF.label: fact

items.text: Raymond James states that through its Private Client Group it provides financial planning, investment advisory, and securities transaction services for which it generally charges either asset-based fees, presented in "Asset management and related administrative fees," or sales commissions, presented in "Brokerage revenues."
items.quote: Through our PCG segment, we provide financial planning, investment advisory, and securities transaction services for which we generally charge either asset-based fees (presented in “Asset management and related administrative fees”) or sales commissions (presented in “Brokerage revenues”).

items.text: Raymond James states its Private Client Group also earns revenues for distribution and related services performed related to mutual and other funds, fixed and variable annuities, and insurance products.
items.quote: The PCG segment also earns revenues for distribution and related services performed related to mutual and other funds, fixed and variable annuities, and insurance products.

items.text: Raymond James states its Private Client Group includes servicing fee revenues from third-party mutual fund and annuity companies whose products it distributes and from banks to which it sweeps a portion of clients' cash deposits as part of the RJBDP multi-bank sweep program.
items.quote: The segment includes servicing fee revenues from third-party mutual fund and annuity companies whose products we distribute and from banks to which we sweep a portion of our clients’ cash deposits as part of the RJBDP, our multi-bank sweep program.

items.text: Raymond James states its Private Client Group also includes net interest earnings primarily on assets segregated for regulatory purposes, margin loans provided to clients, cash balances, and securities borrowing transactions, net of interest paid on client cash balances.
items.quote: The segment also includes net interest earnings primarily on assets segregated for regulatory purposes, margin loans provided to clients, cash balances, and securities borrowing transactions, net of interest paid on client cash balances in the Client Interest Program and securities lending transactions.

items.text: Raymond James states that the majority of assets in Private Client Group fee-based accounts are invested in programs for which its financial advisors provide investment advisory services, and that administrative services are generally performed by its Asset Management segment, which shares a portion of the related revenue.
items.quote: The majority of assets in fee-based accounts within our PCG segment are invested in programs for which our financial advisors provide investment advisory services, either on a discretionary or non-discretionary basis. Administrative services for such accounts (e.g., record-keeping) are generally performed by our Asset Management segment and, as a result, a portion of the related revenue is shared with the Asset Management segment.

items.text: Raymond James states its Asset Management segment earns asset management and related administrative fees for providing asset management, portfolio management and related administrative services to retail and institutional clients, and oversees the portion of fee-based AUA invested in managed programs for PCG clients through AMS.
items.quote: Our Asset Management segment earns asset management and related administrative fees for providing asset management, portfolio management and related administrative services to retail and institutional clients. This segment oversees the portion of our fee-based AUA invested in “managed programs” for our PCG clients through AMS.

a2.RJF.reason: The passages state the revenue streams through which RJF's advisor-led Private Client Group and Asset Management model earns on client assets.

a3.RJF.label: fact

items.text: Raymond James states that Private Client Group asset management and related administrative fees and brokerage revenues are typically correlated with the level of PCG client assets under administration, including those in fee-based accounts, as well as the overall U.S. equity markets.
items.quote: Asset management and related administrative fees and brokerage revenues in this segment are typically correlated with the level of PCG client AUA, including those in fee-based accounts, as well as the overall U.S. equity markets.

items.text: For the quarter ended June 30, 2026, Raymond James states its Private Client Group asset management and related administrative fees increased primarily due to higher assets in fee-based accounts resulting from market appreciation and net new assets driven by financial advisor recruiting and retention, while brokerage revenues increased primarily due to higher client activity and higher trailing revenues from higher client asset values.
items.quote: Asset management and related administrative fees increased $272 million, or 19%, primarily due to higher assets in fee-based accounts at the beginning of the current quarter compared with the prior-year quarter, resulting from market appreciation and net new assets driven by financial advisor recruiting and retention. Brokerage revenues increased $65 million, or 15%, primarily due to higher client activity in the current quarter, as well as higher trailing revenues primarily due to higher client asset values.

items.text: Raymond James states that about 65% of its overall Private Client Group assets are fee-based, and that fee-based assets have grown faster than overall client assets.
items.quote: We're now at 65%, or so of our overall assets in the Private Client Group, are fee-based. We've always really led the industry in fee-based penetration.
items.unit: share of overall Private Client Group assets that are fee-based

items.text: Raymond James states that Private Client Group results can be impacted by changes in the level of client cash balances and by the allocation of client cash balances between the RJBDP, the CIP, and the ESP, because the PCG segment may earn different amounts from each of these client cash destinations.
items.quote: PCG segment results can be impacted by not only changes in the level of client cash balances, but also by the allocation of client cash balances between the RJBDP, the CIP, and the ESP, as the PCG segment may earn different amounts from each of these client cash destinations, depending on multiple factors.

items.text: For the quarter ended March 31, 2026, Raymond James states its Private Client Group account and service fees decreased due to a decrease in RJBDP fees paid to PCG from third-party banks reflecting lower average balances swept and a lower average RJBDP third-party bank yield, partially offset by higher mutual fund service fees from higher average mutual fund assets.
items.quote: Account and service fees decreased $3 million, or 1%, due to a decrease in RJBDP fees paid to PCG from third-party banks which reflects the impacts of lower average balances swept to such banks and the aforementioned reduction in the average RJBDP third-party bank yield, partially offset by higher mutual fund service fees primarily driven by higher average mutual fund assets.

items.text: Raymond James states that PCG servicing fees for clients' deposits swept to banks as part of the RJBDP are variable and fluctuate based on client cash balances in the program, the level of short-term interest rates, and the interest paid to clients.
items.quote: Our PCG segment earns servicing fees for the administrative services we provide related to our clients’ deposits that are swept to banks as part of the RJBDP. These servicing fees are variable in nature and fluctuate based on client cash balances in the program, as well as the level of short-term interest rates and the interest paid to clients on balances in the RJBDP.

a3.RJF.reason: The passages state what drives the advisor-led model's earnings on client assets, which is the RJF side of the comparison.

Raymond James Financial: The 2025 10-K states that its Private Client Group also includes net interest earnings primarily on assets segregated for regulatory purposes, margin loans provided to clients, cash balances, and securities borrowing transactions, net of interest paid on client cash balances.

Raymond James Financial: The Q4 2025 10-Q (period ended December 31, 2025, published February 6, 2026) states that the majority of assets in Private Client Group fee-based accounts are invested in programs for which its financial advisors provide investment advisory services, and that administrative services are generally performed by its Asset Management segment, which shares a portion of the related revenue.

Raymond James Financial: The 2025 10-K states that its Asset Management segment earns asset management and related administrative fees for providing asset management, portfolio management and related administrative services to retail and institutional clients, and oversees the portion of fee-based AUA invested in managed programs for PCG clients through AMS.

Morgan Stanley: On the Q4 2025 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025, published January 15, 2026), management said that the drivers of continued expanded Wealth Management margins are twofold: building fee-based revenues and fee-based assets by introducing clients to the advice-based (advisor-led) model, while self-directed clients generate increasing transactional revenues through investments in E*TRADE.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Trade press reporting published September 30, 2026 states that wealth managers earn revenue on client cash by investing or lending uninvested balances at yields higher than the rates they pay clients, and that when interest rates climb, yields on loans, floating-rate assets, and reinvested fixed-income securities rise, widening the spread that drives net interest income.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Trade press reporting published September 30, 2026 states that Fitch said firms with greater exposure to floating-rate assets, faster reinvestment of maturing holdings, and less reliance on rate-sensitive funding are better positioned to see more immediate net interest income gains.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Trade press reporting published September 30, 2026 states that Raymond James, which holds primarily floating-rate securities and corporate loans alongside certain variable-rate sweep fee arrangements with third-party banks, is positioned to see more immediate earnings benefits when rates rise because its repricing happens faster in response to short-term rate movements.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Trade press reporting published September 30, 2026 states that LPL, which does not operate its own bank and instead places client deposits with partner institutions that pay it a fee, holds roughly 40% of insured cash account balances under variable-rate agreements as of the second quarter of 2026, so a portion of its earnings reprices relatively quickly while the fixed-rate segment lags.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Trade press reporting published September 30, 2026 states that Ameriprise's bank investment portfolio, with a 4.2-year duration and 6% in floating-rate securities, is weighted toward fixed-rate assets, meaning repricing would be more gradual.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: Trade press reporting published September 30, 2026 states that Stifel's commercial, fund-banking and venture deposit mix makes it harder to isolate the revenue contribution from sweep balances specifically, according to Fitch.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the Q4 2025 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025, published January 21, 2026), the CEO said that return on client assets (ROCA) for Managed Investing solutions is two times that of retail, which diversifies the firm's revenue streams.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: The Q3 2025 10-Q (period ended September 30, 2025, published November 7, 2025) states that Schwab's Investor Services segment provides retail brokerage, investment advisory, and banking and trust services to individual investors, and retirement plan and business services, as well as other corporate brokerage services, to businesses and their employees.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: The Q3 2025 10-Q states that Schwab's Advisor Services segment provides custodial, trading, banking and trust, and support services to independent RIAs, independent retirement advisors, and recordkeepers, and that revenues and expenses are attributed to the two segments based on which segment services the client.

Merrill: The 2025 10-K states that client balances managed under advisory and/or discretion of GWIM are AUM and are typically held in diversified portfolios, that fees earned on AUM are calculated as a percentage of clients' AUM balances, and that asset management fees commonly depend on the breadth of the client's relationship.

Merrill: On the Q2 2026 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2026, published July 14, 2026), the CFO stated that the growth in banking relationships and lending balances demonstrates the power of the firm's integrated wealth and banking model, as clients consolidate more of their financial lives with Bank of America.

Merrill: The November 5, 2025 investor day deck states that Merrill's foundational beliefs include that growth of fully advised client relationships drives financial outcomes and that the resilience of the business model creates enduring shareholder value.

Raymond James Financial: The 2025 10-K states that Private Client Group asset management and related administrative fees and brokerage revenues are typically correlated with the level of PCG client assets under administration, including those in fee-based accounts, as well as the overall U.S. equity markets.

Raymond James Financial: The Q2 2026 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026, published August 5, 2026) states that for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, Private Client Group asset management and related administrative fees increased primarily due to higher assets in fee-based accounts resulting from market appreciation and net new assets driven by financial advisor recruiting and retention, while brokerage revenues increased primarily due to higher client activity and higher trailing revenues from higher client asset values.

Raymond James Financial: On the Q2 2025 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2025, published July 23, 2025), management said that about 65% of its overall Private Client Group assets are fee-based, and that fee-based assets have grown faster than overall client assets.

Raymond James Financial: The Q2 2025 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2025, published August 6, 2025) states that Private Client Group results can be impacted by changes in the level of client cash balances and by the allocation of client cash balances between the RJBDP, the CIP, and the ESP, because the PCG segment may earn different amounts from each of these client cash destinations.

Raymond James Financial: The Q1 2026 10-Q (period ended March 31, 2026, published May 6, 2026) states that for the quarter ended March 31, 2026, Private Client Group account and service fees decreased due to a decrease in RJBDP fees paid to PCG from third-party banks reflecting lower average balances swept and a lower average RJBDP third-party bank yield, partially offset by higher mutual fund service fees from higher average mutual fund assets.

Raymond James Financial: The Q2 2026 10-Q states that PCG servicing fees for clients' deposits swept to banks as part of the RJBDP are variable and fluctuate based on client cash balances in the program, the level of short-term interest rates, and the interest paid to clients.

The comparison can be made at a qualitative level on this evidence, but not as a like-for-like quantitative comparison across firms. Schwab, the direct-to-investor brokerage and bank, earns through net interest revenue on client cash, asset management and administration fees, trading revenue, and bank deposit account fees. The advisor-led firms earn primarily through fee-based advice revenue tied to client assets: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management asset management revenues are generally based on the net asset value of the account in which a client is invested; Edward Jones primarily derives revenues from investment advisory and other account service fees, asset-based fees, and commissions; Merrill's fees on AUM are calculated as a percentage of clients' AUM balances; and Raymond James generally charges either asset-based fees or sales commissions in its Private Client Group. The evidence states the driver directly: Morgan Stanley attributes continued expanded Wealth Management margins to building fee-based revenues and fee-based assets in the advisor-led model while self-directed clients generate transactional revenue, and trade reporting notes that wealth managers earn on client cash by investing or lending uninvested balances at yields above what they pay clients. Edward Jones has no driver-specific statement in the provided sources, so the comparison is incomplete for that firm. A like-for-like quantitative comparison is not valid because the firms use different definitions, scopes, units, and periods; for example, Morgan Stanley's basis-point fee rates on Wealth Management fee-based client assets, Raymond James's Private Client Group figures, Merrill's GWIM figures, and Schwab's consolidated revenue sources cannot be ranked or compared on a common basis.

items.text: Capgemini's World Wealth Report states the future of wealth management will be defined by personalization at scale, underpinned by empathetic advisory relationships, with personalization increasingly embedded in the firm through augmented intelligence across every client interaction.
items.quote: The future of wealth management will be defined by personalization at scale, underpinned by empathetic advisory relationships.

items.text: Capgemini states engagement models will evolve so life transitions, liquidity events, and behavioral signals determine when and how firms interact with clients, replacing calendar-driven review cycles with relevance-driven ones.
items.quote: life transitions, liquidity events, and behavioral signals will increasingly determine when and how firms interact with clients, replacing calendar-driven review cycles with relevance-driven ones.

items.text: Capgemini states the wealth management landscape is shifting from selling products to offering personalized, empathetic advice, with future success defined by how well firms understand clients' lifestyles and aspirations rather than just their assets.
items.quote: The wealth management landscape is shifting from selling products to offering personalized, empathetic advice: future success will be defined by how well firms understand clients' lifestyles and aspirations, rather than just their assets.

items.text: Deloitte states agentic AI will do more than improve efficiency and will likely reshape how advice is created, packaged, and delivered.
items.quote: agentic AI will do more than improve efficiency; it will likely reshape how advice is created, packaged, and delivered.

items.text: Wealthtender states the balance of technological enhancement with human oversight represents the future of financial advice.
items.quote: This balance of technological enhancement with human oversight represents the future of financial advice.

items.text: Schwab CEO Rick Wurster states the future Schwab is building is people and AI working together to deliver better outcomes for clients.
items.quote: That is the future we are building. Our people and AI working together to deliver better outcomes for clients.

items.text: Wealthtender states consumers now expect digital-first experiences even for traditional services like financial advice.
items.quote: consumers now expecting digital-first experiences even for traditional services like financial advice.

a1.all.reason: Passages state forward-looking positions about the overall future state of financial advice.

items.quote: One-third of survey participants said an advisor's physical location doesn't matter because they prefer to meet exclusively online.

items.quote: Our multichannel service model delivers award-winning, 24/7 support via online, mobile, telephone, and branch channels

items.quote: One-third of prospects don't care about advisor location, preferring online meetings exclusively.

McKinsey (published February 10, 2025) states that, after a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, fee rates have stabilized according to PriceMetrix by McKinsey, with fee rates for $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships holding steady since 2019. Why it might matter: McKinsey separately anticipates fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.

claims.text: Cerulli (published March 25, 2026) estimates middle-market and mass-affluent households with $100,000 to $2 million in financial assets represent a $25 trillion market of 46.9 million households that seeks involved advisor relationships and benefits from streamlined advisory services at scale. Why it might matter: Cerulli notes wealth management firms have traditionally preferred to begin client relationships only after prospects have reached addressable asset minimums ranging from $250,000 to more than $1 million.

Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states its initiatives include Financial Planning Services for a more personalized experience, and targeting High Net Worth, Workplace, and a new digital platform for Next Generation investors. Why it might matter: Edward Jones states these initiatives aim to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states its multichannel service model delivers 24/7 support via online, mobile, telephone, and branch channels. Why it might matter: Schwab states this ensures clients receive consistent service regardless of asset level or preferred method of engagement.

Bank of America's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states GWIM provides a full set of investment management, brokerage, banking and retirement products, plus comprehensive wealth management solutions for high net worth and ultra high net worth clients. Why it might matter: Bank of America states this is delivered through a high-touch client experience via a network of financial advisors focused on clients with over $250,000 in total investable assets.

Schwab's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) lists managed investing solutions, alternative investments, digital assets, banking, and trust among the products available to clients. Why it might matter: Schwab states its managed investing solutions include customized personal advice for tailored portfolios, specialized planning, and portfolio management.

Morgan Stanley's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states Wealth Management provides a comprehensive array including advisor-led brokerage, investment advisory, custody, cash management, self-directed brokerage, financial and wealth planning, workplace services, securities-based lending, banking, and retirement plan services. Why it might matter: Morgan Stanley states Wealth Management supports individual investors, including high and ultra-high net worth individuals, and businesses and institutions.

Morgan Stanley's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states its businesses are subject to increasing privacy and data protection legal requirements concerning the use and protection of personal information. Why it might matter: Morgan Stanley states these requirements impose mandatory privacy and data protection obligations, including enhanced governance and accountability requirements, and significant fines and litigation risk for noncompliance.

Bank of America's investor day deck (published November 5, 2025) shows its wealth continuum differs by segment: predominantly digital experience for Mass Market, guidance delivered at scale for Mass Affluent, solutions for complex needs for High Net Worth, and managing generational wealth for Ultra High Net Worth. Why it might matter: Bank of America states its wealth management businesses serve 4.7 million clients and have 7% market share.

Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) finds conducting family meetings and maintaining a regular cadence of communication with family members is a key best practice used by 89% of HNW practices surveyed in 2024. Why it might matter: Cerulli says this allows practices to better tackle the issues presented by a significant wealth transfer and provide a full-family advisory approach.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published October 9, 2025) finds wealthy next generation investors seek holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies, plus broader life guidance beyond investment management. Why it might matter: Fidelity says generation X, Y, and Z investors are reshaping the advisor-client relationship as the largest wealth transfer in history unfolds.

Wealthtender (published August 13, 2025) states the balance of technological enhancement with human oversight represents the future of financial advice. Why it might matter: Wealthtender says its data shows consumers are comfortable with AI for administrative tasks and data analysis but uncomfortable with autonomous investment decisions, providing a roadmap for technology implementation.

Wealthtender (published August 13, 2025) states consumers now expect digital-first experiences even for traditional services like financial advice. Why it might matter: Wealthtender anticipates continued growth in AI tool usage for advisor searches and increasing expectations for faster response times and digital-first communications.

Wealthtender's 2025 survey (published August 13, 2025) found one-third of participants said an advisor's physical location doesn't matter because they prefer to meet exclusively online. Why it might matter: Wealthtender says this represents a fundamental change in how financial relationships can work, with the ability to work with the best advisor regardless of geography outweighing the traditional preference for in-person meetings.

Wealthtender (published August 13, 2025) states common advisor fee models include asset-based fees (typically 0.5% to 1.5% annually), hourly rates ($150-$500+ per hour), flat project fees, or monthly subscription fees. Why it might matter: Wealthtender notes financial advisor fees vary significantly based on services provided, asset level, and the advisor's fee structure.

Wealthtender's 2025 survey (published August 13, 2025) finds nearly half of participants expect a response within 24-48 hours, and quality advisors typically respond within 4-24 hours during business hours. Why it might matter: Wealthtender notes that if an advisor takes more than 2-3 business days to respond to an initial inquiry, this may indicate how responsive they will be once someone is a client.

Wealthtender's 2025 survey (published August 13, 2025) finds 72% of consumers will visit the advisor's website and 73% will schedule an introductory call during their advisor search. Why it might matter: Wealthtender notes nearly three-quarters of people want to speak with an advisor directly.

Cerulli (published May 28, 2025) finds fee-based planning is the most preferred form of compensating an advisor, preferred by 36% of affluent investors, yet many still choose commission-based or no-fee services. Why it might matter: Cerulli notes fee-based payment appeals because the advisor's compensation is tied to portfolio performance rather than to selling particular products.

McKinsey (published February 10, 2025) states gen AI can rapidly synthesize information from various sources to prepare advisors for meetings with an overview of a client's portfolio, and that chatbots and virtual assistants can provide 24/7 client service. Why it might matter: McKinsey says gen AI can deliver 6 to 12 percent of time savings for the advisor population by 2034 and, in turn, increase advisor capacity.

Kitces Research (published December 20, 2023) states getting paid appropriately requires advisors to charge a full fee for services delivered, which may require raising fees over time. Why it might matter: Kitces says this is challenging in practice because it implies advisors may not be able to work with all clients and may need to raise their fees over time.

items.text: Schwab's CEO says Schwab is already an AI-enabled company, having used machine learning and AI for years, and that AI will accelerate its strategy by opening new distribution channels and enabling personalized relationships with clients it could not serve person-to-person.
items.quote: Schwab is already an AI-enabled company. We have been using machine learning and AI capabilities for years... AI will accelerate our strategy... AI opens up new distribution channels and allows us to create personalized relationships with clients we have not been able to serve with a person-to- person relationship.

items.text: Schwab's CEO says AI is becoming embedded in everything the firm does and its greatest advantage comes from combining people with AI-powered capabilities to create deeper relationships that scale with clients' needs.
items.quote: it is becoming more embedded in all we do, accelerating our strategy and amplifying our competitive advantages by personalizing client experiences, enhancing productivity, and driving scalable growth. Importantly, we believe our greatest advantage comes from combining people with AI-powered capabilities to create deeper relationships that scale with our clients' needs.

items.text: Raymond James' CEO says AI should help advisers produce more bespoke, tailored insights and save time on administrative tasks so they can spend more time on deeply personal client relationships.
items.quote: something that AI should help down the road because it will help advisers come up with more bespoke tailored insights that advice safe there, save them time on administrative tasks and allow them to spend more time developing those deeply personal relationships with their clients.

items.text: Raymond James' CEO describes its approach to AI in three buckets: supporting infrastructure, resiliency and cybersecurity; increasing efficiency and consistency of service; and helping advisers and bankers provide more bespoke, tailored advice to more clients.
items.quote: the way we think about AI is really in three buckets. The first is to support our infrastructure, the resiliency, the cybersecurity apparatus... Secondly, increasing efficiency and consistency of service... Finally, is to help our financial advisors and bankers provide more bespoke and tailored advice to a larger number of clients.

items.text: Raymond James says it wants to use AI to help its financial professionals and advisers better serve clients, unlike competitors that use technology to go direct to clients around their advisers.
items.quote: we're really wanting to use AI to help our financial professionals and our financial advisors better serve their clients, where many of our competitors have used technology and are planning on using AI to essentially try to get around their financial advisors to go direct to their clients. That is not our goal.

items.text: Raymond James tells its advisers that AI will not replace advisers; advisers who use AI will replace advisers who do not use AI.
items.quote: We say to our advisers, AI will not replace advisers. Advisers who use AI will replace advisers who do not use AI.

items.text: Bank of America's CEO says the firm's view of AI is 'enhanced intelligence' because teammates remain critical to delivering services.
items.quote: Our view of AI is it's enhanced intelligence, that the teammates are going to be critical delivering the services, and therefore, it's an enhanced intelligence, not an artificial intelligence.

items.text: Bank of America says AI is helping wealth management and other relationship-manager bankers search and summarize information to prepare personalized planning and pitches for clients.
items.quote: In wealth management and our other relationship manager banking businesses, AI is helping those relationship managers and advisors search and summarize information, preparing them to deliver personalized planning and personalized pitches to clients for their business and help with their advice.
items.scope: Wealth management and other relationship manager banking businesses

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO says AI is the firm's friend and the latest generation of technology that will be part of the ecosystem.
items.quote: AI is our friend, okay? It is just the latest generation of technology that is going to be part of the ecosystem.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO says AI is additive to its world-class technology and cyber defense, with the best trusted advisers sitting with the client remaining the key.
items.quote: this is something we consider to be additive to what we have, which is world-class technology, world-class cyber defense and then the best trusted advisers sitting with the client. That is ultimately, again, the secret sauce.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO cites the accelerating adoption of AI across the enterprise as a defining theme, with its potential for enhanced efficiencies and productivity only beginning to be realized.
items.quote: The first is the accelerating adoption of artificial intelligence, not only by consumers, but more importantly, across the enterprise, where its potential for enhanced efficiencies and productivity is only beginning to be realized.

items.text: Raymond James says its suite of AI-based tools and technologies is focused on empowering financial advisors and professionals by applying AI to enhance service models in secure, scalable applications.
items.quote: The firm's suite of AI-based tools and technologies is focused on empowering financial advisors and professionals across the firm by applying artificial intelligence to enhance service models in secure, scalable applications.

a1.all.reason: These are the firms' own stated positions and descriptions of how AI relates to advice delivery.

a2.all.label: fact

items.text: Schwab says near-term AI efforts will power client-facing reps and make internal teams more efficient, and longer term AI will meaningfully enhance how it serves and personalizes for clients.
items.quote: In the near term, these AI efforts will help power our client-facing reps as they serve our clients and help make our internal teams more efficient... Over the longer term, we believe AI will meaningfully enhance the way we serve our clients and allow us to reach our clients in an even more personalized way.

items.text: Schwab plans to launch generative search on schwab.com, an Investor AI assistant in June 2026, and AI assistants for service and support, including enabling clients to set beneficiaries with clear handoffs to human agents and strict guardrails.
items.quote: we will be launching a generative search capability... Starting over the summer, we will introduce the first of several AI assistants... Our first iteration of the Investor AI assistant will launch in June... clients will be able to interact with the voice agent to set beneficiaries. We're ensuring clear handoffs to human agents and strict guardrails.

items.text: Schwab plans to meet clients' trust and tax needs with AI-powered capabilities, including wealth.com, and sees opportunities for enhanced experiences and new fee-based offers.
items.quote: We are also now able to meet our clients' trust needs with an AI-powered capability from wealth.com. We will do the same with tax. Over time, these efforts will create opportunities for enhanced experiences and new fee-based offers that will create value we believe our clients will be willing to pay for.

items.text: Schwab plans to roll out an AI-powered thinkorswim assistant and has started a pilot for traders to connect to its MCP layer via the LLM of their choice, beginning with Claude.
items.quote: we are rolling out an AI-powered thinkorswim assistant and have started a pilot for traders to safely and securely connect to our MCP layer via the LLM of their choice. We've started the pilot with Claude and will expand to additional clients and LLMs in the coming months.

items.text: Schwab lists 'Partnering with AI platforms to reach prospective clients' as an AI initiative in development.
items.quote: Partnering with AI platforms to reach prospective clients

items.text: Raymond James says it will continue investing in automation, process improvement and AI as part of its more than $1.1 billion annual technology spend to equip advisers with private wealth tools and deliver deeper, more tailored advice.
items.quote: we'll continue investing in automation, process improvement and AI as part of our more than $1.1 billion annual technology spend.

items.text: Raymond James says it is budgeting for a significant increase in AI expense next year and expects AI to continue to differentiate it over time.
items.quote: We're budgeting for a significant increase in the AI expense next year. We think that over time this will continue to differentiate us.

items.text: Bank of America's CFO expects more technology and intimacy with customers, with AI becoming more agentic versus prompt and more built into the process.
items.quote: the trends will be more technology, more intimacy with the customers more agentic versus prompt more built into the process rather than have it be delivered by teammates doing something, it's part of the process

items.text: Bank of America's CEO says it is working with agent providers to keep the human in the loop before money is moved out of customer accounts.
items.quote: we're working with various agent providers and others to -- like we worked with some of the aggregators to make sure that the customers in control of the decision, the human remains in the loop before money is moved out of their account

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO says its growth plans embed the increasing adoption of AI tools throughout the enterprise and inside its client base.
items.quote: Our growth plans embed the increasing adoption of AI tools throughout the enterprise and inside our client base.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO says the firm is now 'double overweight' to AI and that being part of AI's evolution is the firm's top priority as trusted adviser.
items.quote: I would say we are now double overweight. There is just no question that this is existentially important that we are viewed as a trusted adviser in the middle of the ecosystem... this is absolutely the top priority for the firm as the adviser

items.text: Edward Jones has partnered with Aboon, an AI-driven third-party administrator, and Retirement Plan Advisory Group to develop an end-to-end retirement plan management tool to help its advisers better serve business owners and their employees.
items.quote: Edward Jones has partnered with Aboon, an AI-driven third-party administrator, and Retirement Plan Advisory Group (part of Great Gray Group) to develop an end-to-end retirement plan management tool. The firm hopes the new technology will help its advisors better serve business owners and their employees.

items.text: Edward Jones has taken a minority stake in Quicken, intending to integrate Quicken's personal financial management capabilities to support its value proposition and adviser conversations with clients.
items.quote: Edward Jones announced that they have taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken , with an explicit intention that the investment is a step towards integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones as a way to support their value proposition and advisor conversations with clients.

aspects.keyword_query: fee structure pricing model fee schedule asset-based fee flat fee subscription fee retainer fee performance fee fee compression fee pressure fee reduction fee-based commission-based tiered pricing fee changes

aspects.text: The direction the wealth management industry is heading on pricing transparency, including fee disclosure and clear pricing.
aspects.keyword_query: pricing transparency fee transparency transparent pricing transparent fees fee disclosure pricing disclosure clear pricing fee clarity disclosure requirements Form CRS marketing rule

a1.all.label: fact

items.text: Cerulli states that for the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.
items.quote: For the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.

items.text: Cerulli finds that fee-based payments are preferred by 36% of affluent investors as the form of compensating their advisor.
items.quote: fee-based payments preferred by 36% of affluent investors.

items.text: Cerulli finds that 33% of affluent investors say they compensate their provider via an asset-based fee, 21% use a no-fee platform, and 20% use a commission-based method.
items.quote: 33% of affluent investors say they compensate their provider via an asset-based fee —just three percentage points lower than the 36% who indicated that they prefer this type of fee; 21% use a no-fee platform, and 20% use a commission-based method of payment

items.text: McKinsey states that fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019.
items.quote: fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019

items.text: McKinsey believes fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.
items.quote: We believe fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.

items.text: McKinsey states that after a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, fee rates have stabilized, with $1.0 million to $1.5 million advisory relationships staying at an average of approximately 104 basis points since 2019.
items.quote: After a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013to 2018, fee rates havestabilized... fee rates for $1.0million to $1.5million advisory relationships havestayed at anaverageof approximately 104basis points since 2019.

items.text: Edward Jones states that ongoing fee compression has occurred across the mutual fund industry in recent years and that continued changes in industry fee structures and further compression of management or distribution fees could materially affect its results.
items.quote: the ongoing fee compression that has occurred across the mutual fund industry in recent years... Continued changes in industry fee structures, further compression of management or distribution fees

items.text: Deloitte states that competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare, while margin expansion is possible for firms that execute and maintain pricing.
items.quote: competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.

items.text: Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry states the firm wants a profitable, competitive and fair pricing structure and would be flexible and open to evolving with industry pricing, fees and payout based on competitive pressures and client preferences.
items.quote: we want to have a profitable and competitive and fair pricing structure... if that evolves in the industry based on competitive pressures and competitive dynamics and client preferences... we would be flexible and open to evolving

items.text: Schwab CFO Michael Verdeschi states the company's model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service.
items.quote: Our model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience or service.

items.text: InvestmentNews reports that financial advice and wealth management companies' advisors charge clients annual fees in the neighborhood of 1% of assets, and it is widely feared that AI-based financial planning functions will erode that fee.
items.quote: financial advisors charge clients annual fees in the neighborhood of 1% of assets for their work... It is widely feared that financial planning functions based on AI will erode that fee
items.scope: financial advice and wealth management companies

items.text: McKinsey states that if the marginal cost of generating tax analysis, scenario modeling, portfolio commentary and meeting documentation collapses, then operating leverage, advisor capacity and fee durability require rigorous reexamination.
items.quote: If the marginal cost of generating tax analysis, scenario modeling, portfolio commentary, and meeting documentation collapses, then operating leverage, advisor capacity, and fee durability require rigorous reexamination.

items.text: Raymond James states the increase in non-discretionary asset-based program assets was due in part to the continued trend of clients moving to fee-based accounts from transaction-based accounts.
items.quote: the continued trend of clients moving to fee-based accounts from transaction-based accounts

items.text: Raymond James CEO Paul Shoukry states fee-based assets have grown faster than overall assets and are now about 65% of Private Client Group assets, and that the firm has always led the industry in fee-based penetration.
items.quote: We're now at 65%, or so of our overall assets in the Private Client Group, are fee-based. We've always really led the industry in fee-based penetration.
items.unit: percent of Private Client Group assets

items.text: Edward Jones states asset-based fee revenue growth was due to growth in advisory programs driven by the continued increase in investment of client dollars into advisory programs.
items.quote: the continued increase in investment of client dollars into advisory programs

items.text: InvestmentNews reports that platform fees showing up at large distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry.
items.quote: all these platform tolls showing up at the giant distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry.

items.text: Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick states an important indicator of wealth management momentum is fee-based flows, which reached $123 billion in 2024.
items.quote: An important indicator of wealth management momentum is fee-based flows, which reached an exceptional $123 billion in 2024.

items.text: Bank of America states Merrill Wealth Management revenue growth was partially offset by the impact of lower AUM pricing.
items.quote: partially offset by the impact of lower AUM pricing

a1.all.reason: Passages state the industry's and specific firms' direction on fee structures, fee models, fee levels and fee compression.

a2.all.label: fact

items.text: Wealthtender research states fee transparency tops the trust list, with 73% of survey participants saying transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility.
items.quote: Fee transparency tops the trust list... Nearly three-quarters (73%) of survey participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility.

items.text: Wealthtender research states 38% of survey participants identified lack of fee transparency as a red flag.
items.quote: Lack of fee transparency was identified as a red flag by 38% of survey participants.

items.text: Wealthtender research states many advisors avoid discussing fees upfront, creating an opportunity for transparent advisors, and recommends fee transparency practices such as website fee pages, first-call honesty, and written proposals.
items.quote: Many advisors avoid discussing fees upfront, creating an opportunity for transparent advisors.

items.text: Merrill states it has added disclosure, including as to associated conflicts of interest, regarding new Support Fees and optional data reporting services fees it anticipates beginning to receive as of January 1, 2027.
items.quote: We have added disclosure, including as to associated conflicts of interest, regarding new fees (Support Fees)... We have added disclosure regarding optional data reporting services (Data Analytics)...

items.text: Schwab states it is required under the Investment Advisers Act to provide clients with disclosure brochures describing its investment advisory and financial planning services, including the fees charged and conflicts of interest, and to notify clients of material changes.
items.quote: CS&Co. is required under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940... to provide clients with disclosure brochures that describe our investment advisory and fnancial p lanning services, i ncluding how these services work, the fees charged, and important conficts of i nterest.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that under Department of Labor ERISA regulations it is required to provide certain information regarding its services and compensation to retirement plan fiduciaries at the outset and at least annually.
items.quote: MSWM is required to provide certain information regarding our services and compensation to assist fiduciaries and plan sponsors... This information is provided to you at the outset of your relationship with us... It is also provided at least annually

items.text: InvestmentNews reports the broader debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue, with the SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures unlikely to fade from client conversations.
items.quote: the broader debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue. The SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures... is unlikely to fade from client conversations any time soon.

items.text: Merrill's fee disclosure acknowledges that the Support Fee can limit the range of products available to clients and that support fees will be a factor in whether products are made available.
items.quote: Merrill's recent fee disclosure 'acknowledges that the support fee can limit the range of products available to clients,' and that 'support fees will be a factor in whether products are made available'

items.text: Edward Jones states it will disclose to clients the accounts making up their Pricing Group upon request.
items.quote: Each account can only be in one Pricing Group, and we will disclose to you the accounts making up your Pricing Group upon request.

items.text: InvestmentNews reports that as a condition of a NASAA-led settlement, firms must certify that their commission policies and supervisory procedures have been revised to ensure all charges are fair and reasonable going forward.
items.quote: the firms must certify that their commission policies and supervisory procedures have been revised to ensure all charges are fair and reasonable going forward.

a2.all.reason: Passages state the direction on pricing transparency, including fee disclosure and clear pricing, for the industry and for specific firms.

items.text: Edward Jones describes a new digital platform initiative as focused on attracting and retaining 'Next Generation investors.'
items.quote: a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

a7.EDJ.reason: Edward Jones management uses the term 'Next Generation investors' and describes them as the target of a new digital platform.

a8.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states its branch office model serves clients through deep, personal relationships and comprehensive advice and planning, and offers investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions, and financial planning offerings.
items.quote: The Partnership's branch office model is designed to serve clients through deep, personal relationships and comprehensive advice and planning ... The Partnership offers a variety of different solutions to clients, including investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions and financial planning offerings.

items.text: Edward Jones offers the Edward Jones Insured Bank Deposit Program, an interest-bearing cash management solution with FDIC insurance coverage.
items.quote: the Edward Jones Insured Bank Deposit Program (the "IBD Program"), which is an interest-bearing cash management solution for clients that offers Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") insurance coverage

items.text: Edward Jones has a dedicated team to design accessible digital experiences for clients and colleagues.
items.quote: The Partnership has a dedicated team to design accessible digital experiences for clients and colleagues.

items.text: Edward Jones is pursuing a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.
items.quote: a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

a8.EDJ.reason: Passages describe Edward Jones's current advice model, product solutions, cash solution, accessible digital experiences, and a digital platform aimed at Next Generation investors.

a9.EDJ.label: fact

items.quote: a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

a9.EDJ.reason: The passage states a priority of attracting and retaining Next Generation investors via a new digital platform.

a10.EDJ.label: different_quantity

items.text: Edward Jones states it competes with firms offering discount services and zero commissions for stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products, and with fintech companies offering internet- and mobile-based platforms.
items.quote: The Partnership also competes with firms of all sizes offering discount services, usually with lower levels of personalized service to individual clients, including major competitor brokerage firms that offer zero commissions for purchases and sales of stocks, ETFs and other brokerage products. ... The Partnership also faces competition from "fintech" companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms.

items.text: Edward Jones states the financial services industry includes firms of all sizes providing personalized services and enhanced digital experiences, including artificial intelligence and lower-cost robo-advice.
items.quote: The financial services industry continues to innovate and evolve technologically, with an increasing number of firms of all sizes providing personalized services and enhanced digital experiences for clients, including the utilization of artificial intelligence technologies and lower cost, computer-based "robo-advice".

a10.EDJ.differs_because: The passages name general competitive threats (discount/zero-commission brokers, fintech, robo-advice), not competition named specifically for serving younger investors.
a10.EDJ.reason: No passage names competitors specifically for younger investors, so the related broader competition statements are labeled different_quantity.

a11.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones reported net new assets decreased 10% in the second quarter of 2025, attributing outflows in part to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.
items.quote: Net new assets decreased by 10% compared to the second quarter of 2024, continuing a downward trend which can be attributed to higher asset outflows. These outflows are impacted by a variety of factors, including, without limitation, an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm, macroeconomic volatility, inflation and consumer spending.

items.text: Edward Jones reported net new assets decreased 4% in the first nine months of 2025, with outflows continuing a downward trend influenced in part by an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.
items.quote: Net new assets decreased 4% in the first nine months of 2025. ... The outflows relative to the prior-year period continue an increasing downward trend influenced by several factors, including an aging client base, generational wealth transfers outside the firm, macroeconomic volatility, inflationary pressures, and shifts in consumer spending.

a11.EDJ.reason: Edward Jones attributes net new asset declines to generational wealth transfers outside the firm, indicating lost ground as wealth passes to younger generations.

claims.text: Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab's CEO cited industry research showing Gen Z is 45% more likely than Millennials to start investing by age 21.
Schwab: On Schwab's second-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2025), Schwab said young investors want to think about how to pay off their college debt and how to buy a house.
Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said younger investors at Schwab are highly engaged in building their wealth over the long term.

Bank of America Private Bank research published June 17, 2026 reports that 67% of younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45) believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns.

Bank of America Private Bank research published June 17, 2026 states younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45) are reshaping how wealth is built and diversified, embracing alternative investments and emerging technologies.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 17, 2026 reports crypto ranks as the number one wealth-creation opportunity for young wealthy investors, with 29% ranking it number one.

Bank of America Private Bank research published June 18, 2024 reports that younger investors (ages 21 to 43) believe it is no longer possible to achieve above-average investment returns by investing solely in traditional stocks and bonds.

FINRA research published December 4, 2025 reports younger respondents are much more likely than older respondents to invest for reasons other than long-term profits; half or more of those under 35 say they invest for social responsibility, entertainment, and social activity reasons.

FINRA research published December 4, 2025 reports younger investors' enthusiasm for social responsibility, entertainment, and social activity reasons for investing has declined noticeably relative to 2021.
FINRA research published December 4, 2025 reports that among those who have purchased meme stocks or other viral investments, 66% cite entertainment as a reason for investing.
FINRA research published December 4, 2025 reports that among those who have purchased meme stocks or other viral investments, 65% cite social activity as a reason for investing.

Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, and Schwab is the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.

Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said one reason younger investors (Gen Z) turn to Schwab is that Schwab meets them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

Schwab: On Schwab's second-quarter 2026 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2026), Schwab's CEO said growth in young investors was partly started by the removal of commissions, which brought people with less money into the market.

Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said younger traders turn to Schwab because they recognize trading's potential to help build wealth over time.
Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said crypto will be great for clients and will certainly appeal to young investors.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 17, 2026 reports younger investors allocate nearly half as much to stocks as older generations.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 17, 2026 reports younger investors allocate 13% to crypto, more than older investors.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 17, 2026 reports 58% of younger investors currently own crypto, up from 49% in 2024.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 17, 2026 reports 92% of younger investors either own crypto or are interested in owning it.

Bank of America Private Bank research published June 17, 2026 reports 88% of younger investors say they are likely to allocate more to alternatives in the next few years, compared with 15% of Boomers and Silents.
FINRA research published December 4, 2025 reports younger investors (under 35) are much more likely to own individual stocks than mutual funds: 82% own individual stocks.
FINRA research published December 4, 2025 reports 47% of investors under 35 own mutual funds, versus 82% who own individual stocks.
FINRA research published December 4, 2025 reports 68% of investors aged 18-34 have an account that allows options trading.
FINRA research published December 4, 2025 reports 43% of investors aged 18-34 have traded options.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 18, 2024 reports younger investors (ages 21-43) allocate 17% of their investment portfolios to alternatives, versus 5% for older investors.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 18, 2024 reports younger investors (ages 21-43) allocate 14% of their portfolios to crypto.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 18, 2024 reports younger investors (ages 21-43) allocate 28% of their portfolios to stock.

Bank of America Private Bank research published June 18, 2024 reports 47% of younger high-net-worth investors' (ages 21-43) portfolios are in stocks and bonds, far lower than 74% for investors over 44.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 18, 2024 reports most (93%) younger high-net-worth investors say they plan to allocate more to alternatives in the next few years.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 18, 2024 reports nearly half (49%) of younger high-net-worth investors own cryptocurrencies.
Bank of America Private Bank research published June 18, 2024 reports another 38% of younger high-net-worth investors are interested in owning cryptocurrencies.

Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said one-third of retail households that created a financial plan within the last two years are under age 40.

Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said younger traders turn to Schwab because it offers the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service they need.
Schwab: On Schwab's third-quarter 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab said younger investors (Gen Z) learn about finances primarily through social media and family.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states its branch office model serves clients through deep, personal relationships and comprehensive advice and planning, and offers investment advisory programs, brokerage and retirement accounts, cash and lending solutions, and financial planning offerings.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it offers the Edward Jones Insured Bank Deposit Program, an interest-bearing cash management solution with FDIC insurance coverage.
Edward Jones: Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it has a dedicated team to design accessible digital experiences for clients and colleagues.
Edward Jones: Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it is targeting Next Generation investors through a new digital platform.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones's second-quarter 2025 10-Q (period ended June 27, 2025) reported net new assets decreased 10% compared to the second quarter of 2024, attributing outflows in part to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones's third-quarter 2025 10-Q (period ended September 26, 2025) reported net new assets decreased 4% in the first nine months of 2025, with outflows continuing a downward trend influenced in part by an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) discloses a planned new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors. Why it might matter: Edward Jones's second-quarter 2025 10-Q reported net new assets decreased 10% compared to the second quarter of 2024, attributing outflows in part to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.

items.text: UBS research reports that, when choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list, at 79%.
items.quote: When choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list (79%).

items.text: UBS research reports that 41% of next-generation respondents value a wealth manager's ability to fully understand the next generation's needs.
items.quote: Another plus point for advisors is their ability to fully understand the next generation's needs (41%).

items.text: UBS research reports priorities vary by gender: women emphasize wealth managers' experience (90%), frequent engagement (35%), and early commitment to the next generation (40%), while men are more likely to prioritize advisors with a deep understanding of their financial goals (49%).
items.quote: Women emphasize wealth managers' experience (90%), frequent engagement (35%), and early commitment to the next generation (40%). Men are more likely to prioritize advisors with a deep understanding of their financial goals (49%).

items.text: UBS research finds the next generation want advisors with not just technical know-how, but the ability to build rapport with the family and communicate clearly with every generation, and partners who can connect them to new ideas, networks, and real-world experiences.
items.quote: The next generation want advisors with not just technical know-how, but the ability to build a rapport with the family and communicate clearly with every generation. They want partners who can connect them to new ideas, networks, and real-world experiences.

items.text: Cerulli reports younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, so financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.
items.quote: Younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages (e.g., E*TRADE, Fidelity), meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

items.text: Cerulli reports that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.
items.quote: While older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.

items.text: Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study finds wealthy next-generation households are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies.
items.quote: generation X, Y, and Z investors are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies.

a1.all.reason: Passages state criteria and attributes next-generation and younger investors consider when choosing an advisor (expertise, understanding needs, rapport, planning benefits, control).

a2.all.label: fact

items.text: UBS research finds the next generation rarely relies on a single source of guidance for succession planning; peer insights are most popular (27%), just ahead of wealth managers (21%), with tax advisors (16%), lawyers (14%), and family officers (13%) ranking roughly even.
items.quote: Peer insights are most popular (27%), just ahead of wealth managers (21%). Sources of advice from other advisors such as family officers (13%), lawyers (14%) and tax advisors (16%) rank roughly even.

items.text: UBS research finds younger adults (22 to 25 years) rely most on peers (57%) for succession-planning advice, while older respondents turn increasingly to formal legal advice.

claims.text: UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) reports that when choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the next generation's wish list, at 79%.
UBS: The same UBS research report (published April 22, 2026) reports that 41% of next-generation respondents value a wealth manager's ability to fully understand the next generation's needs.

UBS: The same UBS research report (published April 22, 2026) reports priorities vary by gender among next-generation respondents: women emphasize wealth managers' experience (90%), frequent engagement (35%), and early commitment to the next generation (40%), while men are more likely to prioritize advisors with a deep understanding of their financial goals (49%).

Cerulli: Cerulli's research (published October 29, 2025) reports that younger investors typically are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, so financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

Cerulli: Cerulli's research (published October 29, 2025) reports that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.

Fidelity: Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published October 9, 2025) finds wealthy next-generation households are reshaping the advisor-client relationship with a focus on holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies.

UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) finds the next generation rarely relies on a single source of guidance for succession planning; peer insights are most popular (27%), just ahead of wealth managers (21%), with tax advisors (16%), lawyers (14%), and family officers (13%) ranking roughly even.

UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) finds younger adults (22 to 25 years) rely most on peers (57%) for succession-planning advice, while older respondents turn increasingly to formal legal advice.

FINRA: FINRA investor research (published December 4, 2025) finds investors under 35 are somewhat less likely than older investors to rely on financial professionals and much more likely to use information from friends, family and colleagues; word of mouth from friends/family/colleagues is the most frequently mentioned source of investment information, used by 85% of investors under 35.

Schwab: On Schwab's Q3 2025 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025; transcript published October 16, 2025), the CEO stated that Gen Z learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and that Schwab meets them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

Wealthtender: Wealthtender's survey (published August 13, 2025; 2025 survey of respondents ages 35-64) finds the most-planned resource for finding a financial advisor is referrals from friends or family (62%), with search engines such as Google or Bing next (49.8%).

Wealthtender: Wealthtender's survey (published August 13, 2025; 2025 survey of respondents ages 35-64) finds 25% plan to use AI tools like ChatGPT to start their advisor search; about one-third (32%) will use online advisor directories; social media platforms influence about 22%; and educational events (online webinars 19%, in-person seminars 18%) also play a role.

Bank of America Private Bank: Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 17, 2026) finds 65% of younger investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor; the study defines younger investors as Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45.
Bank of America Private Bank: The same 2026 study finds 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios.
UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) finds most next-generation respondents favor a blended approach to communicating (83%), combining digital convenience with in-person interaction.
UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) finds two-thirds (67%) of next-generation respondents say a strong personal connection with their advisor is important.
UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) finds more than half (56%) of next-generation respondents want advisors who can build trusted relationships across generations.

UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) finds the next generation want advisors with not just technical know-how, but the ability to build rapport with the family and communicate clearly with every generation.

UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) finds continuity is important in succession planning: 41% of next-generation respondents prefer to work with their family's existing bank, while 31% want a new provider and 29% are open to switching.

UBS: UBS's research report (published April 22, 2026) quotes a next-generation portfolio manager saying good partners aren't easy to find, and when they find someone committed and trustworthy they want to work with them for the long term.

Wealthtender: Wealthtender's survey (published August 13, 2025; 2025 survey of respondents ages 35-64) finds nearly half of participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors leading them to choose one advisor over another.

Wealthtender: Wealthtender's survey (published August 13, 2025; 2025 survey of respondents ages 35-64) finds that before contacting an advisor, 62% of people want to know the advisor's fee structure first, alongside areas of specialization (64%).

Wealthtender: Wealthtender's survey (published August 13, 2025; 2025 survey of respondents ages 35-64) finds fee transparency tops the trust list: 73% of participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility.

Bank of America Private Bank: Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 17, 2026) was an online survey by Escalent among 1,431 wealthy U.S. individuals aged 21 or older with at least $3 million in investable assets (excluding primary residence), fielded January 8 to February 5, 2026.

Bank of America Private Bank: The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans finds 65% of younger investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, 47% use AI to research companies or markets, and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI.

Bank of America Private Bank: The 2024 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published June 18, 2024) was an online survey by Escalent among 1,007 HNW U.S. respondents aged at least 21 with at least $3 million in investable assets (excluding primary residence), with a margin of error of +/-3% at 95% confidence.
Fidelity: Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published October 9, 2025) compares the evolving preferences and expectations of wealthy next-generation households with those of baby boomers.

Wealthtender: The Wealthtender 2025 study (published August 13, 2025) surveyed 500 U.S. adults with household incomes over $100,000, selected from 1,557 screened individuals ages 35-64, focused on those who don't have a financial advisor or are considering a change and anticipate hiring an advisor within five years.

Wealthtender: Wealthtender's 2025 study key takeaways include: 97% plan to interview multiple advisors and 96% will do further research online before hiring; 83% research the advisor's reputation via online reviews and awards; the two most important pre-contact pieces of information are areas of specialization (64%) and fee/pricing structure (62%).

UBS: UBS's research report on what the next generation looks for in a wealth manager (published April 22, 2026) finds experience and expertise top the next generation's wish list (79%), with 56% wanting advisors who build trusted relationships across generations.

items.text: Schwab states that roughly 80% of retail assets are held by ultra-high net worth and high net worth households, and that it is well positioned to continue serving future generations when that wealth is passed on.
items.quote: Roughly 80% of retail assets are held by ultra-high net worth and high net worth households, and we are well positioned to continue serving future generations when that wealth is passed on.
items.unit: of retail assets held by U/HNW households

items.quote: ~75% Assets Retained in a Wealth Transfer Event 3

a4.SCHW.reason: The deck gives a wealth-transfer retention figure and the transcript states retention is extremely high, addressing whether heirs retain assets and stay with Schwab.

a5.SCHW.label: fact

items.text: Schwab describes itself as built to win across generations.
items.quote: Built to win across generations.

items.text: Schwab says it is well positioned to serve future generations when wealth is passed on and is winning assets with all generations.
items.quote: we are well positioned to continue serving future generations when that wealth is passed on. Our retention rate around wealth transfers is extremely high, and we are winning assets with all generations.

items.quote: The next generations of investors
